32889: Son of Jehoiada of Kabzeel (2 Sam 23:20). Over the Cherethites and Pelethites (2 Sam 8:18). Honoured among the thirty (2 Sam 23:22-23). Supported Solomon (1 Kgs 1:36-37). Put over the army in Joab's place (1 Kgs 2:35). His father is called a chief priest (1 Chr 27:5).
32890: Terse, fearless and obedient; a soldier who answers 'Amen' and acts.
32897: He serves as one of David's two chief priests.
32898: Carries the ark and returns it
32899: When David flees Absalom, Zadok brings the ark, but David sends it back: if God favours him, he will bring him back to it.
32901: Through his son Ahimaaz he passes intelligence to David.
32903: He anoints Solomon with oil from the tabernacle at Gihon, and the people shout 'Long live King Solomon!'
32905: Solomon puts him in Abiathar's place.
32906: Zadok was a priest who served David alongside Abiathar and stayed loyal through Absalom's revolt. When Adonijah tried to seize the throne, Zadok sided with Solomon and anointed him king. Solomon then made him sole chief priest, and his descendants, the Zadokites, led the Jerusalem priesthood for centuries. Ezekiel singles them out as the faithful priests, and the later Sadducees probably take their name from him.
32907: Son of Ahitub, priest with Abiathar (2 Sam 8:17). Brought and returned the ark (2 Sam 15:24-29). Anointed Solomon (1 Kgs 1:39). Replaced Abiathar (1 Kgs 2:35). Descended from Aaron through Eleazar (1 Chr 6:4-8). The sons of Zadok alone may come near to God in Ezekiel's temple (Ezek 44:15).
32908: Some scholars suggest Zadok was originally a Jebusite priest of Jerusalem whom David absorbed, and that the Aaronic genealogy was added later; others accept the Chronicler's genealogy (debated).
32910: The name of the Sadducees probably comes from Zadok, and the Qumran community called its priests 'sons of Zadok' (scholarly-consensus on the Qumran usage).
32911: Calm, loyal and ceremonious; a priest who trusts God with outcomes.
32914: keeper of the ephod for David
32915: last of Eli's line in high office
32917: When Saul's man Doeg kills the priests of Nob, Abiathar alone escapes to David, who takes responsibility and protects him.
32919: With the ephod, a priestly object used for seeking God's yes-or-no answers, he helps David inquire of the LORD.
32921: With Zadok he brings out the ark and then stays in Jerusalem to help David.
32923: He supports Adonijah's claim. Solomon spares his life because he served David, but sends him home to Anathoth, fulfilling the word against Eli's house.
32924: Abiathar, son of Ahimelech, was the only priest to survive Saul's massacre at Nob. He joined David as a fugitive and served him faithfully for decades, carrying the ephod and later sharing the chief priesthood with Zadok. In old age he backed Adonijah for the throne. Solomon banished him to Anathoth, and the narrator notes that this fulfilled the prophecy against Eli's family. Jesus mentions him in connection with David eating the holy bread.
32925: Son of Ahimelech, escaped to David (1 Sam 22:20). Brought the ephod (1 Sam 23:6). Priest with Zadok (2 Sam 15:29). Supported Adonijah (1 Kgs 1:7). Banished to Anathoth 'to fulfil the word of the LORD concerning the house of Eli' (1 Kgs 2:26-27). Named by Jesus (Mark 2:26).
32927: 1 Samuel 21 says Ahimelech was priest when David ate the bread. Some explain Mark's 'in the time of Abiathar' as referring to the section of scripture or the era of the better-known priest; others see a slip by Mark or a copyist (debated).
32928: His banishment is read as the long fulfilment of judgment on Eli's corrupt house (1 Sam 2:30-36). Jeremiah, a priest from Anathoth, may have descended from him (speculative).
32929: Weathered and loyal, a survivor who has seen a king's violence; cautious about the future.
32934: Lower date from Josephus' Tyrian king list
32941: He sends cedar, carpenters and stonemasons to build a house for David.
32942: Treaty with Solomon for the temple
32943: He supplies cedar and cypress from Lebanon in exchange for wheat and oil; the two kings make a treaty.
32945: Solomon gives him twenty towns in Galilee. Hiram calls them 'Cabul', meaning roughly 'good for nothing'.
32947: His sailors crew Solomon's ships from Ezion-geber to Ophir, bringing gold.
32948: Hiram was the king of Tyre, the great Phoenician port, and a friend and trading partner of David and Solomon. He supplied the cedar timber and skilled craftsmen for David's palace and Solomon's temple and shared in Solomon's sea trade. Josephus, using Tyrian records, places his reign in the tenth century BC. He is different from Hiram (Huram-abi) the bronze-worker who cast the temple's pillars.
32949: Sent materials for David's house (2 Sam 5:11). 'Always loved David' (1 Kgs 5:1). Blessed the LORD for giving David a wise son (1 Kgs 5:7). Treaty with Solomon (1 Kgs 5:12). Received twenty Galilean towns (1 Kgs 9:11-13). Another Hiram, a craftsman from Tyre, made the bronze work (1 Kgs 7:13-14).
32950: Josephus (*Against Apion* 1.17-18) cites Tyrian annals naming Hiram son of Abibaal; most historians accept a real Hiram I in the tenth century, though exact dates depend on how the Tyrian list is calculated (debated).
32951: Businesslike, generous and diplomatic; a merchant-king who speaks in terms of fair exchange.
32955: Tears his cloak into twelve pieces
32956: Meeting Jeroboam outside Jerusalem, he tears his new cloak into twelve pieces and gives him ten: God will tear ten tribes from Solomon's son because of Solomon's idolatry.
32957: Foretells the end of Jeroboam's house
32958: Old and blind, he recognises Jeroboam's disguised wife and tells her their sick son will die and Jeroboam's dynasty will be wiped out for its idolatry.
32959: Ahijah was a prophet from Shiloh who announced the split of Solomon's kingdom. He dramatically tore his cloak into twelve pieces and gave ten to Jeroboam, promising him the northern tribes and a lasting dynasty if he obeyed God. When Jeroboam turned to golden calves, the now-blind Ahijah told his wife that their son would die and the dynasty would end, which happened under Nadab.
32960: A prophet from Shiloh (1 Kgs 11:29). Symbolic tearing of the cloak (1 Kgs 11:30-31). Promised Jeroboam a 'sure house' if he obeyed (1 Kgs 11:38). Prophesied against Jeroboam's house (1 Kgs 14:10-11), fulfilled by Baasha (1 Kgs 15:29). Chronicles mentions his written prophecy (2 Chr 9:29).
32961: Solemn and vivid; acts out his message, then speaks hard words without softening them.
32968: Before battle he calls on Jeroboam's army not to fight the LORD, the God of their fathers, pointing to David's covenant and Judah's lawful priests.
32970: Surrounded by an ambush, Judah cries to the LORD and the priests blow trumpets; Israel is routed and Abijah takes Bethel and other towns.
32971: Abijah (called Abijam in Kings) reigned over Judah for three years, about 913 to 911 BC. Kings gives a negative verdict: he 'walked in all the sins of his father' and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD, yet God kept a lamp burning in Jerusalem for David's sake. Chronicles instead records his speech and victory over Jeroboam, showing a king who at least appealed to the LORD in battle. The text's overall verdict is mixed.
32972: Reigned three years in Jerusalem; walked in his father's sins (1 Kgs 15:1-3). Kept on the throne for David's sake (1 Kgs 15:4-5). War with Jeroboam (1 Kgs 15:7). His mother was Maacah daughter of Abishalom (1 Kgs 15:2), also called Micaiah daughter of Uriel (2 Chr 13:2). Defeated Jeroboam 'because they relied on the LORD' (2 Chr 13:18). Had fourteen wives (2 Chr 13:21). In Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:7).
32973: Kings and Chronicles are often read as complementary: a king with a generally poor record who nevertheless relied on the LORD in one crisis.
32974: Many scholars see the speech in Chronicles as the Chronicler's own composition setting out his theology of the Davidic kingship and the Jerusalem priesthood (debated).
32975: Confident and rhetorical, fond of appeals to tradition and legitimacy.
32985: He becomes king and does what is right in the LORD's eyes. He drives out the male cult prostitutes, removes his fathers' idols and foreign altars, and commands Judah to seek the LORD.
32986: Ten years of peace and building
32987: The land is quiet, and he uses the peace to build fortified cities with walls, towers and gates, and to raise a large army.
32989: A vast army under Zerah the Cushite invades. Asa prays, 'LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak; help us, for we rely on you.' Judah wins at Mareshah and pursues the enemy to Gerar.
32991: The prophet Azariah son of Oded tells him, 'The LORD is with you while you are with him.' Asa removes idols, repairs the altar and gathers Judah and northern migrants to swear a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart.
32993: He removes his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she made an obscene image for Asherah, and burns the image in the Kidron Valley.
32995: Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah, a few miles north of Jerusalem, to cut off traffic to and from Judah.
32997: Asa sends silver and gold from the temple and palace to Ben-hadad of Damascus, who breaks his treaty with Baasha and raids northern Israel. Baasha withdraws, and Asa uses his stones to fortify Geba and Mizpah.
32999: Hanani tells him he relied on the king of Aram instead of the LORD: 'the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth' to support those whose hearts are fully his. Asa angrily puts Hanani in the stocks and oppresses some of the people.
33001: In his thirty-ninth year he develops a severe disease in his feet, and 'even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but the physicians'.
33003: He dies in his forty-first year and is buried in a tomb he had cut for himself, laid on a bier of spices, with a very great fire made in his honour.
33004:
Asa was the third king of Judah after the kingdom split, reigning about forty-one years (roughly 911/910 to 870/869 BC on Edwin Thiele's widely used chronology). The verdict of the text is that he 'did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done' and that his heart was 'wholly true to the LORD all his days', though the high places, local hilltop shrines, were not all removed. He is one of only a handful of Judean kings compared favourably with David.

His early reign was a model of reform. He cleared out idols and cult prostitutes, deposed his own grandmother Maacah as queen mother for making an Asherah image, and led a national covenant renewal. When a huge army under Zerah the Cushite invaded, he prayed a short, honest prayer of dependence, and Judah won.

His later years tell a different story. When Baasha of Israel blockaded Judah, Asa emptied the temple treasury to bribe Ben-hadad of Damascus into attacking Israel. It worked politically, but the seer Hanani told him he had relied on a foreign king instead of God. Asa jailed the prophet and oppressed his people, and when his feet became diseased he sought physicians but not the LORD. Chronicles uses his life to show that a strong start does not guarantee a faithful finish.
33005:
Son of Abijah; reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 15:8-10). Did right as David did; removed cult prostitutes and idols; deposed Maacah (1 Kgs 15:11-13). High places not removed, yet his heart was wholly true (1 Kgs 15:14). Bribed Ben-hadad against Baasha (1 Kgs 15:18-20). Diseased in his feet in old age (1 Kgs 15:23).

Chronicles adds ten years of peace (2 Chr 14:1), the victory over Zerah (2 Chr 14:9-15), Azariah's prophecy and the covenant (2 Chr 15:1-15), Hanani's rebuke and Asa's harsh response (2 Chr 16:7-10), and that he sought physicians not the LORD (2 Chr 16:12). He appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:7-8).
33007: Chronicles shapes Asa's life around 'seeking' and 'relying on' the LORD: blessing when he relies on God (2 Chr 14:11; 16:8), trouble when he relies on Aram. Many see this as the Chronicler's teaching on immediate moral consequences.
33009: Kings says the high places were not removed (1 Kgs 15:14), while Chronicles says he removed them (2 Chr 14:3-5) yet also that they were not removed from Israel (2 Chr 15:17). Common harmonisations: he removed pagan shrines but not local shrines to the LORD; or he removed them early but they returned; or 'Israel' in 2 Chr 15:17 means the north. Others see two sources with different emphases (debated).
33011: Some read 2 Chr 16:12 as condemning reliance on doctors instead of God; most commentators say the fault was seeking help without God, not medicine itself, and some suggest the 'physicians' may have used pagan healing practices (debated).
33012: The Talmud (Sotah 10a) connects his foot disease to conscripting scholars and even bridegrooms for labour in 1 Kgs 15:22, reading the punishment as fitting the offence (tradition).
33013: Bold reform, even against his own grandmother (1 Kgs 15:13)
33014: Humble prayer of dependence in crisis (2 Chr 14:11)
33015: Led the people in wholehearted covenant renewal (2 Chr 15:12-15)
33016: Used temple treasure to buy a foreign alliance (1 Kgs 15:18)
33017: Imprisoned the prophet who rebuked him (2 Chr 16:10)
33018: Oppressed some of the people (2 Chr 16:10)
33019: Did not seek the LORD in illness (2 Chr 16:12)
33020: Azariah's word, 'if you seek him he will be found by you' (2 Chr 15:2)
33021: Baasha's blockade at Ramah and the choice to pay Ben-hadad (2 Chr 16:1-3)
33023:
Asa reigned early in the divided kingdom, when Judah and Israel were often at war over their shared border just north of Jerusalem. Aram (Syria), based in Damascus, was emerging as the main power to the north, and both Hebrew kingdoms courted it. Egypt to the south had recently raided Judah under Shishak (1 Kgs 14:25-26), and Zerah's invasion may reflect an Egyptian-backed force from the south (scholarly views differ on who Zerah was).

Asa's long reign overlapped with several northern kings: Jeroboam I, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri and the start of Ahab. Chronicles' figures for his thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years (2 Chr 15:19; 16:1) clash with Kings, where Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth year (1 Kgs 16:8). Some scholars, following Thiele, count those years from the division of the kingdom rather than Asa's accession; others suspect a copying error (debated).
33024: Asa was remembered as one of Judah's good kings, and his son Jehoshaphat continued his reforms (1 Kgs 22:43). His story is a classic biblical warning about finishing well: a man of great early faith who in later years trusted political deals and resented correction. Hanani's line about the eyes of the LORD running through the whole earth (2 Chr 16:9) became a widely quoted promise. Jeremiah later mentions the cistern Asa built at Mizpah (Jer 41:9).
33025: Decisive and earnest in his early years, praying in short plain sentences; later guarded, defensive and quick to take offence at criticism.
33031: While besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon he is killed by Baasha, who then wipes out the whole house of Jeroboam, as Ahijah had foretold.
33032: Nadab, son of Jeroboam I, ruled Israel for about two years (around 910 to 909 BC). The verdict of the text is that he did evil and walked in his father's sin of calf worship. He was murdered by Baasha during a siege, ending Jeroboam's dynasty after only two kings.
33033: Reigned two years; did evil, walking in Jeroboam's way (1 Kgs 15:25-26). Killed by Baasha at Gibbethon (1 Kgs 15:27-28). His family destroyed according to Ahijah's word (1 Kgs 15:29-30).
33034: Little recorded; imagine a young heir confident in a throne that was already doomed.
33038: He kills Nadab and wipes out Jeroboam's family.
33040: He fortifies Ramah against Asa, but withdraws when Ben-hadad of Damascus, bribed by Asa, attacks northern Israel.
33041: Condemned by Jehu son of Hanani
33042: The prophet tells him that because he followed Jeroboam's sins, his house will be swept away like Jeroboam's.
33043: Baasha, from the tribe of Issachar, killed Nadab and made himself king of Israel, reigning about twenty-four years (around 909 to 886 BC) from Tirzah. The verdict of the text is that he did evil and kept Jeroboam's calf worship. He fought Asa of Judah throughout his reign. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani foretold that his dynasty would fall, and his son Elah was murdered by Zimri after two years.
33044: Son of Ahijah of Issachar; killed Nadab (1 Kgs 15:27). Reigned twenty-four years at Tirzah and did evil (1 Kgs 15:33-34). War with Asa all their days (1 Kgs 15:16). Fortified Ramah (1 Kgs 15:17). Jehu son of Hanani's oracle (1 Kgs 16:1-4). Zimri destroyed his house (1 Kgs 16:11-13).
33045: Hard, ambitious soldier-king; speaks the language of opportunity and force.
33047: Uncertain; perhaps 'servant of the LORD' or 'my sheaf'
33054: When Zimri murders King Elah, the army at Gibbethon makes its commander Omri king. He besieges Tirzah and Zimri burns the palace over himself.
33056: Half the people follow Tibni; after several years Omri's side wins.
33058: He buys the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and builds a new capital, which remains Israel's capital until its fall.
33059: Omri was an army commander who became king of Israel during a civil war and reigned about twelve years (around 885 to 874 BC, including years of rivalry with Tibni). The verdict of the text is that he 'did more evil than all who were before him'. Kings gives him only a few verses, but he was one of Israel's most important rulers politically: he built Samaria as a new capital and founded a dynasty so famous that Assyrian records called Israel 'the house of Omri' long after it ended. The Moabite Mesha Stele says Omri oppressed Moab.
33060: Commander made king by the army (1 Kgs 16:16). Defeated Zimri and Tibni (1 Kgs 16:17-22). Reigned twelve years, six at Tirzah (1 Kgs 16:23). Bought and built Samaria (1 Kgs 16:24). Did more evil than all before him (1 Kgs 16:25-26). Micah condemns 'the statutes of Omri' (Mic 6:16).
33061: The Mesha Stele (about 840 BC) and Assyrian inscriptions ('Bit-Humri', house of Omri; Jehu called 'son of Omri' on the Black Obelisk) confirm his importance (scholarly-consensus). Archaeologists also credit the Omrides with major building at Samaria, Megiddo, Hazor and Jezreel, though dating some of it is debated.
33062: Shrewd, practical and ambitious; a general turned statesman who thinks in terms of land, walls and treaties.
33067: He joins Jehoshaphat in building ships for trade, but they are wrecked; Jehoshaphat later refuses a second venture.
33069: Injured in a fall through a lattice in his upper room, he sends to ask Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, whether he will recover. Elijah intercepts the messengers: he will die.
33071: Two companies sent to arrest Elijah are consumed by fire; the third captain begs for mercy, and Elijah goes to the king and repeats the sentence. Ahaziah dies.
33072: Ahaziah, son of Ahab and Jezebel, reigned over Israel for about two years (around 853 to 852 BC by inclusive counting). The verdict of the text is that he did evil, following his father, his mother and Jeroboam, and served Baal. After a fall he sought a foreign god's oracle instead of the LORD, and Elijah announced his death. He had no son, so his brother Jehoram succeeded him.
33073: Reigned two years over Israel; did evil and served Baal (1 Kgs 22:51-53). Moab rebelled after Ahab's death (2 Kgs 1:1). Fell and consulted Baal-zebub (2 Kgs 1:2). Died according to Elijah's word; no son, Jehoram reigned (2 Kgs 1:17).
33074: Imperious yet fearful; a sick king who sends soldiers to fix what only repentance could.
33080: With Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom he marches against Moab. Elisha promises water and victory for Jehoshaphat's sake, but when Mesha sacrifices his son on the wall, the allies withdraw.
33082: Receiving a letter asking him to heal Naaman, he tears his clothes, suspecting a trick, until Elisha asks for Naaman to be sent to him.
33084: During a terrible famine under Aramean siege he blames Elisha and seeks his life; Elisha foretells relief the next day, and the Arameans flee in the night.
33086: Wounded fighting Hazael at Ramoth-gilead, he recovers at Jezreel. Jehu shoots him with an arrow on Naboth's land, fulfilling Elijah's word against Ahab.
33087: Jehoram (also spelled Joram), son of Ahab, reigned over Israel for about twelve years (around 852 to 841 BC). The verdict of the text is that he did evil, 'though not like his father and mother', because he removed Baal's sacred pillar, but he kept Jeroboam's sins. His reign is full of Elisha stories: the Moab campaign, Naaman, and the siege of Samaria. Jehu killed him at Jezreel, ending Omri's dynasty.
33088: Reigned twelve years; did evil but removed the pillar of Baal (2 Kgs 3:1-3). Campaign against Moab (2 Kgs 3:6-27). Probably the unnamed 'king of Israel' in several Elisha stories (2 Kgs 5-7). Killed by Jehu (2 Kgs 9:24). The synchronisms of 2 Kgs 1:17 and 2 Kgs 3:1 differ, which Thiele explains by a co-regency in Judah (debated).
33089: Erratic and defensive; swings between panic, blame and grudging respect for the prophet.
33094: Once secure on the throne he kills all six brothers and some officials.
33096: Edom throws off Judah's rule and sets up its own king; Libnah also revolts.
33098: A letter from Elijah condemns him for following Ahab's house and killing his better brothers and warns of a disease of the bowels.
33100: Philistines and Arabians plunder his house and take his sons except the youngest. He dies in agony and 'departed with no one's regret'.
33101: Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, reigned over Judah for eight years, probably as co-regent with his father from about 853 BC and alone from about 848 to 841 BC. He married Athaliah, daughter of Ahab, and the verdict of the text is that he 'walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done'. He murdered his brothers, lost Edom, and died of a painful disease unmourned. Yet the LORD would not destroy David's house, because of his covenant promise.
33102: Reigned eight years; married Ahab's daughter and did evil (2 Kgs 8:16-18). The LORD spared Judah for David's sake (2 Kgs 8:19). Edom revolted (2 Kgs 8:20-22). Killed his brothers (2 Chr 21:4). Elijah's letter (2 Chr 21:12-15). Died unmourned, not buried in the kings' tombs (2 Chr 21:19-20). In Jesus' genealogy as Joram (Matt 1:8).
33104: 2 Kings 3 suggests Elijah had been taken up before this time, so some say the letter was written in advance, some that Elijah's departure is narrated out of chronological order, and others that Chronicles is using a later tradition (debated).
33105: Suspicious and ruthless; a man who secures power by removing rivals.
